title: Deadlocks in Go: The Hidden Trap of String Formatting
content:
Concurrency in Go is powerful but treacherous. It’s easy to assume that locking a mutex and formatting an error message are innocuous actions. But combine the two under certain conditions, and you have a recipe for a deadlock.

Let’s explore a subtle mistake that can cause your Go program to halt unexpectedly — deadlocks caused by string formatting inside methods that also use mutexes.

The Setup: A Simple Customer Struct

Here’s a seemingly safe struct:

type Customer struct {
    mutex sync.RWMutex
    id    string
    age   int
}

You want to safely update a customer’s age and format error messages when invalid data is passed. You also want to implement fmt.Errorf to print the customer's data.

func (c *Customer) UpdateAge(age int) error {
    c.mutex.Lock()
    defer c.mutex.Unlock()

    if age < 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("age should be positive for customer %v", c)
    }

    c.age = age
    return nil
}

func (c *Customer) String() string {
    c.mutex.RLock()
    defer c.mutex.RUnlock()
    return fmt.Sprintf("id %s, age %d", c.id, c.age)
}

The Problem: fmt.Errorf + Mutex = 💣

The bug is hiding in this line:

return fmt.Errorf("age should be positive for customer %v", c)

Because c implements the String interface, %v triggers a call to c.String(). But UpdateAge already holds a write lock, and String() tries to acquire a read lock on the same mutex. Since Go’s sync.RWMutex doesn’t allow a thread to acquire a read lock while holding a write lock (even reentrantly), the goroutine deadlocks.

You’ll see this nasty error at runtime:

fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

The Fix: Lock Only When Necessary

Avoid locking the mutex unless you know the operation is safe. Validate first, then lock:

func (c *Customer) UpdateAge(age int) error {
    if age < 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("age should be positive for customer %v", c)
    }

    c.mutex.Lock()
    defer c.mutex.Unlock()

    c.age = age
    return nil
}

This way, the String() method is never called inside a critical section. You still get the necessary validation and keep your application free from deadlocks.

Bonus Lesson: Always Test Edge Cases

This issue wouldn’t be caught unless you test invalid inputs. Writing a test case for a negative age would have exposed the deadlock early:

func TestUpdateAge_Negative(t *testing.T) {
    c := &Customer{id: "123"}
    err := c.UpdateAge(-5)
    if err == nil {
        t.Fatal("expected error for negative age")
    }
}

Takeaway

Deadlocks in Go aren’t always about complex goroutine interactions. Sometimes, they arise from simple, everyday code — like formatting an error. The key takeaway? Always think twice before formatting structs that may hold locks, and avoid calling methods that acquire locks inside a locked section.

Validate first. Lock second. Format wisely.

title: Expecting Deterministic Behavior Using select and Channels in Go
content:
When working with Go’s concurrency primitives, especially select statements, it's easy to assume that they behave like regular switch statements. This assumption can lead to subtle bugs, particularly when we expect deterministic behavior.

The Problem

Consider a common scenario with two channels:

  • messageCh: Receives new messages to process using buffered channels.
  • disconnectCh: Signals a disconnection event.

You might write something like this to handle both:

for {
    select {
    case v := <-messageCh:
        fmt.Println(v)
    case <-disconnectCh:
        fmt.Println("disconnection, return")
        return
    }
}

The intent is to prioritize processing all messages before reacting to disconnections. But this code is flawed if you assume the select will prioritize messageCh because it's listed first.

What’s Really Going On?

The Go spec states:

If one or more of the communications can proceed, a single one that can proceed is chosen via a uniform pseudo-random selection.

This means that if both channels are ready, Go randomly picks one. In other words, ordering of case statements doesn’t imply priority.

Demonstration

Suppose:

for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
    messageCh <- i
}
disconnectCh <- struct{}{}

You might expect all 10 messages to print before disconnection. But output like this is possible:

0
1
2
3
4
disconnection, return

Only half the messages are received because select chose the disconnect randomly once both were ready​.

Solutions

1. Use Unbuffered Channels

If there’s one producer goroutine, switch to unbuffered channels. The producer blocks until the receiver is ready, ensuring all messages are received before disconnection is possible.

2. Use a Single Channel with a Union Type

Define a struct type like:

type Event struct {
    Message     *string
    Disconnected bool
}

Then send events in order over a single channel. Channel ordering is guaranteed FIFO.

3. Handle Disconnection Then Drain Messages

For multiple producers, consider:

for {
    select {
    case v := <-messageCh:
        fmt.Println(v)
    case <-disconnectCh:
        for {
            select {
            case v := <-messageCh:
                fmt.Println(v)
            default:
                fmt.Println("disconnection, return")
                return
            }
        }
    }
}

This inner for/select loop drains messageCh after receiving a disconnect signal. The default makes sure the loop exits when the channel is empty​.

Key Takeaways

  • select chooses ready cases randomly — not based on their order in code.
  • Use unbuffered channels or unified channels to control behavior deterministically.
  • Consider a post-disconnect draining mechanism when using buffered channels and multiple producers.

Understanding how Go’s select truly behaves is critical to writing correct, deterministic concurrent code.

title: Propagating an Inappropriate Context in Go: Pitfalls and Solutions
content:
Context propagation is a core principle in Go’s concurrency model. It allows developers to pass cancellation signals, deadlines, and values — such as correlation IDs — throughout a call chain. However, mismanaging context propagation, especially in asynchronous operations, can lead to subtle and hard-to-debug issues. In this article, we’ll explore the problem of propagating an inappropriate context, illustrate the potential pitfalls with a concrete example, and discuss effective strategies to mitigate these issues.

Understanding Context Propagation

In Go, a context is represented by the context.Context interface, which defines methods for retrieving a deadline, a cancellation signal, and key/value pairs. When used properly, contexts help manage timeouts and cancellations, ensuring that goroutines do not run indefinitely and that resources are cleaned up appropriately.

The interface is defined as follows:

type Context interface {
    Deadline() (deadline time.Time, ok bool)
    Done() <-chan struct{}
    Err() error
    Value(key any) any
}

Contexts are meant to be propagated from parent to child, ensuring that when a parent context is canceled, all child operations are also terminated. However, there are cases where propagating the parent context can lead to unintended consequences.

The Problem: Asynchronous Operations and Context Cancellation

Consider an HTTP handler that processes a request and, after sending the response, asynchronously publishes a message to a Kafka topic. The handler might use the HTTP request’s context for both processing the request and for the asynchronous publication:

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    response, err := doSomeTask(r.Context(), r)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }

    go func() {
        err := publish(r.Context(), response)
        // Handle err appropriately
    }()

    writeResponse(response)
}

At first glance, this seems like an efficient way to reuse the context. However, the context attached to the HTTP request is designed to be canceled in several scenarios:

  • When the client disconnects.
  • If the HTTP/2 request is explicitly canceled.
  • Crucially, when the response has been fully written to the client.

In the above example, if the HTTP response is written before or during the asynchronous publication, the context passed to the publish function may already be canceled. This can result in a race condition where the publication is either allowed to complete successfully or is aborted unexpectedly, leading to inconsistent behavior.

Why Propagating an Inappropriate Context is Problematic

The core issue here is that the asynchronous operation (i.e., the Kafka publication) relies on a context that might be canceled by design. If the cancellation signal is propagated to an operation that should continue independently of the HTTP request lifecycle, it can lead to premature termination of the publication. Essentially, the cancellation of the HTTP context — while appropriate for ending the client’s request — should not necessarily apply to downstream asynchronous tasks.

Strategies for Mitigating the Issue

Using a Background Context

A straightforward solution is to decouple the asynchronous operation from the HTTP request’s cancellation by using an empty context:

err := publish(context.Background(), response)

While this approach ensures that the asynchronous operation is not prematurely canceled, it has a significant drawback: any valuable context values (e.g., correlation IDs for distributed tracing) are lost, potentially hampering debugging and monitoring efforts.

Creating a Custom Detached Context

A more refined solution is to create a custom context that retains the useful values from the parent context but detaches the cancellation signal. This can be achieved by implementing a wrapper around the original context. Consider the following custom detach type:

type detach struct {
    ctx context.Context
}

func (d detach) Deadline() (time.Time, bool) {
    return time.Time{}, false
}

func (d detach) Done() <-chan struct{} {
    return nil
}

func (d detach) Err() error {
    return nil
}

func (d detach) Value(key any) any {
    return d.ctx.Value(key)
}

By overriding the Deadline, Done, and Err methods, the custom context effectively ignores cancellation and timeout signals. However, it still delegates the Value method to the original context, preserving any embedded metadata such as correlation IDs. With this custom context, the publish function can be called as follows:

err := publish(detach{ctx: r.Context()}, response)

Now, even if the HTTP request context is canceled, the asynchronous operation will continue executing, and it will still have access to any relevant values from the original context.

Conclusion

Propagating an inappropriate context in asynchronous operations can introduce subtle bugs, especially when the parent context is designed to be canceled as soon as the HTTP response is sent. While using context.Background() might seem like an easy fix, it can lead to loss of important context values. The preferred approach is to implement a custom detached context that preserves useful metadata while avoiding the pitfalls of premature cancellation.

By understanding the nuances of context propagation and applying these strategies, Go developers can build more robust and reliable concurrent applications. This example underscores the importance of carefully considering context propagation to ensure that asynchronous tasks execute as intended, without unintended interruptions due to cancellation signals .

title: Error Management in Go
content:
Error management is a fundamental aspect of building robust and observable applications. In Go, error handling follows a unique paradigm compared to traditional exception-based approaches seen in languages like Java or Python. Instead of using try/catch blocks, Go functions typically return errors as normal values, making error handling explicit and predictable.

This article explores the common mistakes developers make while handling errors in Go and provides best practices to improve code reliability.

Understanding When to Panic

Panic in Go is a built-in function that immediately stops the program’s execution and unwinds the call stack until a recover function is found. While panics are useful in unrecoverable situations, they should not be used as a standard error-handling mechanism.

When to Use Panic

  • When the program encounters an unrecoverable error (e.g., failing to load a critical configuration file).
  • When a function is used incorrectly by a developer (e.g., passing an invalid argument).

Using Panic Incorrectly

func divide(a, b int) int {
    if b == 0 {
        panic("division by zero")
    }
    return a / b
}

A better approach would be to return an error:

func divide(a, b int) (int, error) {
    if b == 0 {
        return 0, errors.New("division by zero")
    }
    return a / b, nil
}

Wrapping Errors for Context

Since Go 1.13, the fmt.Errorf function provides a %w directive to wrap errors. This allows developers to add context to errors while preserving the original error.

This wrapping ensures that the caller can extract the original error using errors.Is or errors.As.

Example

func openFile(filename string) error {
    _, err := os.Open(filename)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to open file %s: %w", filename, err)
    }
    return nil
}

Checking Error Types and Values Correctly

Go provides errors.Is and errors.As for comparing errors, which should be used instead of direct equality checks.

Checking Error Types

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")

func findUser(id int) error {
    return fmt.Errorf("user %d: %w", id, ErrNotFound)
}

func main() {
    err := findUser(42)
    if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
        fmt.Println("User not found!")
    }
}

Checking Error Values

Using errors.As to extract specific error types:

type ValidationError struct {
    Msg string
}

func (e *ValidationError) Error() string {
    return e.Msg
}

func validate(input string) error {
    return &ValidationError{Msg: "Invalid input"}
}

func main() {
    err := validate("bad input")
    var vErr *ValidationError
    if errors.As(err, &vErr) {
        fmt.Println("Validation error occurred:", vErr.Msg)
    }
}

Avoiding Duplicate Error Handling

Handling an error multiple times can introduce unintended behavior. Instead of logging and returning an error at multiple points, propagate the error and handle it at a single location.

Example of Handling an Error Twice (Incorrect)

func fetchData() error {
    err := someOperation()
    if err != nil {
        log.Println("operation failed:", err)
        return err
    }
    return nil
}

A better approach is to handle logging at a single place:

func fetchData() error {
    return someOperation()
}

func main() {
    err := fetchData()
    if err != nil {
        log.Println("Error occurred:", err)
    }
}

Handling Defer Errors

Errors in deferred functions are often ignored, but they should be handled explicitly.

Incorrect: Ignoring Defer Errors

defer file.Close()

Correct: Handling Defer Errors

defer func() {
    if err := file.Close(); err != nil {
        log.Printf("failed to close file: %v", err)
    }
}()

Ignoring Errors Explicitly

If an error is intentionally ignored, it should be done explicitly using the blank identifier (_):

_ = someFunction()

This makes it clear that the error is being ignored intentionally rather than overlooked.

Conclusion

Error handling in Go is explicit, making it easier to understand how errors propagate through the system. By avoiding common mistakes like using panic improperly, failing to wrap errors, or handling errors multiple times, developers can write more robust and maintainable Go applications. Following best practices like using errors.Is, errors.As, and handling errors in deferred functions ensures better error observability and debugging.

title: Mastering Slice Initialization in Go: Why It Matters More Than You Think
content:
When working with Go, slices are part of our daily toolkit. They are efficient, flexible, and straightforward — until they’re not. One of the most overlooked performance pitfalls in Go is inefficient slice initialization, and the cost of getting it wrong can sneak up on you in unexpected ways.

In this article, we’ll dive into:

  • Why default slice initialization can hurt performance
  • Optimize slice allocations
  • Comparing using Benchmark
  • When it makes sense to prioritize readability over raw performance

The Problem with simple Slice Initialization

Consider a common scenario: converting a slice of one type (Foo) into another (Bar). Here's a simple implementation:

func convert(foos []Foo) []Bar {
    bars := make([]Bar, 0)
    for _, foo := range foos {
        bars = append(bars, fooToBar(foo))
    }
    return bars
}

At first glance, this seems fine. We’re initializing an empty slice and appending as we go. But here’s the catch: under the hood, Go is working much harder than it needs to.

What’s happening internally?

  1. We start with an empty slice (make([]Bar, 0)).
  2. Each time we append and fill the backing array, Go allocates a new, larger array — doubling the capacity each time it’s exceeded.
  3. Each new allocation copies the existing elements to the new array.

⚠️ The hidden cost:

For a slice with, say, 1,000 elements, Go may allocate 10 backing arrays and copy over 1,000 elements as the slice grows. This creates unnecessary work for both your CPU and the garbage collector.

Optimizing Slice Initialization

There’s no reason to make Go work this hard. If you know the number of elements you’ll add to a slice, you can optimize your initialization in two simple ways.

Option 1: Predefine the capacity

func convert(foos []Foo) []Bar {
    n := len(foos)
    bars := make([]Bar, 0, n)
    for _, foo := range foos {
        bars = append(bars, fooToBar(foo))
    }
    return bars
}

Why it helps:
By setting the capacity to n, Go preallocates enough space for all the elements, avoiding repeated allocations.

Option 2: Predefine the length

func convert(foos []Foo) []Bar {
    n := len(foos)
    bars := make([]Bar, n)
    for i, foo := range foos {
        bars[i] = fooToBar(foo)
    }
    return bars
}

Why it helps:
This is even slightly faster. We predefine the length, and instead of appending, we assign directly to each index — avoiding the minor overhead of append.

🏁 The Benchmark Results:

With 1 million elements, the difference becomes clear:

Method                  Time(ns/op)         Relative Speed
Empty slice + append    49,739,882          Slowest 🚨
Capacity + append       13,438,544          Faster ✅
Length + index assign   12,800,411          Faster 🏆

🤔 But why use capacity + append if length + index is faster?

Good question! Sometimes, readability matters more than micro-optimization.

func collectAllUserKeys(
    cmp Compare,
    tombstones []tombstoneWithLevel,
) [][]byte {
    keys := make([][]byte, 0, len(tombstones)*2)
    for _, t := range tombstones {
        keys = append(keys, t.Start.UserKey)
        keys = append(keys, t.End)
    }
}

The developers could have used pre-defined length and indexed assignments. But that approach adds more complex indexing math, making the code harder to read:

keys := make([][]byte, len(tombstones)*2)
for i, t := range tombstones {
    keys[i*2] = t.Start.UserKey
    keys[i*2+1] = t.End
}

In this case, since the function isn’t performance-critical, they prioritized clarity over speed.

What if the length is unknown?

Sometimes the future length of a slice depends on runtime conditions:

func convert(foos []Foo) []Bar {
    var bars []Bar
    for _, foo := range foos {
        if something(foo) {
            bars = append(bars, fooToBar(foo))
        }
    }
    return bars
}

When the number of elements is unpredictable, initializing with a rough capacity estimate can help, especially if you expect the condition to be true most of the time. But there’s no strict rule here — it’s a balance between CPU usage and memory consumption.

Key Takeaways

  • If you know the final length: Use make([]T, length) and assign by index.
  • If you know the final capacity but prefer appending: Use make([]T, 0, capacity) and use append.
  • If you don’t know the length: Start with an empty slice, but consider an estimated capacity if conditions suggest heavy usage.
  • Prioritize readability unless the code is performance-sensitive.
  • Benchmark your code if performance matters — you might be surprised by the impact!

👨🏻‍💻 Conclusion

Go gives us powerful control over slices, but with great power comes the responsibility to optimize where it counts. The difference between a well-initialized slice and a naive one could mean faster code, fewer allocations, and less GC pressure.

So next time you’re initializing a slice, pause and ask yourself: Do I know how big this will get?

title: The Functional Options Pattern in Golang
content:
In Go programming, one of the common pitfalls highlighted in 100 Go Mistakes and How to Avoid Them is not using the functional options pattern.

This design approach is particularly effective for managing optional parameters in APIs, offering a cleaner, more maintainable, and extensible solution compared to other approaches. Below, we explore the functional options pattern, compare it with alternative methods, and explain why it stands out as the superior choice.

What is the Functional Options Pattern?

The functional options pattern is a design technique that simplifies the configuration of APIs or functions by using functional constructs to apply options to a configuration struct. Instead of exposing configuration structs directly or relying on overloaded function signatures, this pattern encapsulates configuration logic in a structured and flexible way.

Key Components:

  1. Unexported Configuration Struct: Holds the internal state and default values.
  2. Functional Options: Functions that modify the configuration struct.
  3. Chaining Options: Users can pass multiple options to customize behavior in a concise and readable manner.

Why Use the Functional Options Pattern?

  1. Improved API Usability: Avoids long, complex parameter lists and provides a clear way to set only the options you need.
  2. Flexibility: Users can easily customize behavior without being forced to specify unnecessary defaults.
  3. Extensibility: Adding new options in the future does not require breaking changes to the API.
  4. Readability: The code becomes self-documenting, as options are explicitly named and applied.

Implementation Example

Here’s a simple implementation of the functional options pattern in Go:

package main

import "fmt"

// Unexported struct to hold configuration options
type options struct {
    timeout   int
    retries   int
    debugMode bool
}

// Functional option type
type Option func(*options)

// Functional options
func WithTimeout(timeout int) Option {
    return func(o *options) {
        o.timeout = timeout
    }
}

func WithRetries(retries int) Option {
    return func(o *options) {
        o.retries = retries
    }
}

func WithDebugMode(debug bool) Option {
    return func(o *options) {
        o.debugMode = debug
    }
}

// Function that applies options
func NewClient(opts ...Option) {
    // Default configuration
    config := &options{
        timeout:   30,
        retries:   3,
        debugMode: false,
    }

    // Apply functional options
    for _, opt := range opts {
        opt(config)
    }

    // Use the configured options
    fmt.Printf("Client Config: %+v
", config)
}

func main() {
    // Create a client with custom options
    NewClient(WithTimeout(60), WithRetries(5), WithDebugMode(true))
}

Other Approaches to Configuration Management

1. Direct Struct Usage:

  • Description: Expose a configuration struct directly, allowing users to set fields manually.
  • Drawbacks: Leads to tight coupling, makes it harder to enforce defaults, and complicates future changes.

Example:

package main

import "fmt"

type Config struct {
    Timeout   int
    Retries   int
    DebugMode bool
}

func NewClient(config Config) {
    fmt.Printf("Client Config: %+v
", config)
}

func main() {
    config := Config{
        Timeout:   60,
        Retries:   5,
        DebugMode: true,
    }
    NewClient(config)
}

2. Overloaded Function Signatures

  • Description: Use multiple function signatures to handle optional parameters.
  • Drawbacks: Quickly becomes confusing and error-prone as the number of optional parameters grows.

Example:

package main

import "fmt"

func NewClient(timeout int, retries int, debugMode bool) {
    fmt.Printf("Client Config: Timeout=%d, Retries=%d, DebugMode=%t
", timeout, retries, debugMode)
}

func main() {
    // Overloaded function call
    NewClient(60, 5, true)
}

Conclusion

While the functional options pattern is powerful, it may not always be necessary. For simple functions with only one or two parameters, using this pattern might add unnecessary complexity. Evaluate the trade-offs based on the specific use case.

📚 References

  • 100go
  • 100-go-mistakes

title: [Springboot — Redis] How to improve Spring boot Performance using Caching
content:
[Springboot — Redis] How to improve Spring boot Performance using Caching

In this step-by-step guide, we’ll delve into optimizing Spring Boot performance through caching. By strategically caching frequently accessed data, we can significantly enhance response times and overall efficiency. Whether you’re new to caching or seeking advanced techniques, this article will provide practical insights to elevate your Spring Boot application’s performance.

You can get the app here.

Redis Connection

Once you’ve cloned the repository from the provided link, our journey begins with an exploration of the RedisConfig.

The RedisConfig class serves as the backbone for seamlessly integrating Redis caching into our Spring Boot application. Let's break down its key components.

Firstly, the lettuceConnectionFactory method configures the connection to the Redis server. It utilizes the Lettuce client to establish a connection based on the provided Redis host.

@Bean
RedisConnectionFactory lettuceConnectionFactory(@Value("${redis.host}") final String host) {
    final var redisUri = RedisURI.create(host);
    redisUri.setVerifyPeer(false);

    final var redisConfig = new RedisStandaloneConfiguration(redisUri.getHost(), redisUri.getPort());
    return new LettuceConnectionFactory(redisConfig);
}

Next, we define two methods for configuring Redis cache settings. The customRedisKeyCacheConfig method sets up custom cache configurations for specific keys, such as 'product', with a defined time-to-live (TTL) duration and disables caching of null values.

@Bean
public Map<String, RedisCacheConfiguration> customRedisKeyCacheConfig() {
    final var map = new HashMap<String, RedisCacheConfiguration>();
    map.put("product", RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
            .entryTtl(Duration.ofSeconds(10_000))
            .disableCachingNullValues());

    return map;
}

Meanwhile, the defaultRedisCacheConfiguration method establishes default cache settings, including a TTL of 3 minutes.

@Bean
public RedisCacheConfiguration defaultRedisCacheConfiguration() {
    return RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
            .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(3))
            .disableCachingNullValues();
}

The redisCacheManager method creates a RedisCacheManager instance, utilizing the previously configured Redis connection factory and cache configurations. It allows for both default and custom cache configurations.

@Bean
public RedisCacheManager redisCacheManager(final RedisConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory,
                                           final RedisCacheConfiguration defaultRedisCacheConfiguration,
                                           final Map<String, RedisCacheConfiguration> customRedisKeyCacheConfig) {
    final var builder = RedisCacheManager.builder(redisConnectionFactory);
    builder.cacheDefaults(defaultRedisCacheConfiguration);
    customRedisKeyCacheConfig.forEach(builder::withCacheConfiguration);
    return builder.build();
}

Lastly, the cacheResolver method defines a cache resolver, enabling Spring's caching annotations to interact with Redis cache. This resolver utilizes the RedisCacheManager to resolve cache operations effectively.

@Bean
public CacheResolver cacheResolver(final RedisCacheManager redisCacheManager) {
    return new SimpleCacheResolver(redisCacheManager);
}

CacheTestingController

The CacheTestingController class exemplifies the practical application of caching within our Spring Boot application. Let's delve into its functionality

Each endpoint corresponds to a specific caching operation:

The productById method, annotated with @GetMapping and @Cacheable(value = "product"), retrieves product information by ID. This method is cached with the key "product", ensuring that subsequent requests for the same product ID are served from the cache, avoiding repeated database queries.

@GetMapping("/product/cacheable/{id}")
@Cacheable(value = "product")
public ProductExampleOutput productById() throws InterruptedException {
    System.out.println("Finding product in database");
    Thread.sleep(1_000L);
    return new ProductExampleOutput("123", "productExample", 10.5, LocalDateTime.now());
}

After you call this endpoint you can check inside the redis the key stores and the TTL configured.

Similarly, the customerById method retrieves customer information by ID, with caching enabled using the key customer.

@GetMapping("/customer/cacheable/{id}")
@Cacheable(value = "customer")
public CustumerExampleOutput customerById() throws InterruptedException {
    System.out.println("Finding customer in database");
    Thread.sleep(500L);
    return new CustumerExampleOutput("John", new Random().nextInt(), LocalDateTime.now());
}k

The customerCreate method, annotated with @PostMapping and @CacheEvict(value = "customer", allEntries = true), simulates the creation of a new customer and evicts the corresponding cache entry for the customer cache, ensuring that the cache is updated upon new customer creation.

@PostMapping("/customer/evict/{id}")
@CacheEvict(value = "customer", allEntries = true)
public CustumerExampleOutput customerCreate() throws InterruptedException {
    System.out.println("Creating customer in database");
    Thread.sleep(1_000L);
    return new CustumerExampleOutput("John", 45, LocalDateTime.now());
}

Lastly, the carById method, annotated with @GetMapping and @CachePut(value = "car"), retrieves car information by ID. Unlike @Cacheable, @CachePut always invokes the method and updates the cache with the returned value, making it suitable for scenarios where the method's result needs to be cached regardless of previous caching.

@GetMapping("/car/put/{id}")
@CachePut(value = "car")
public CarExampleOutput carById() throws InterruptedException {
    System.out.println("Finding car in database");
    Thread.sleep(3_500L);
    return new CarExampleOutput("Hi lux", "978", LocalDateTime.now());
}
Each method simulates database retrieval by printing a message and pausing execution for a specified duration using Thread.sleep.

Additionally, three record classes (ProductExampleOutput, CustomerExampleOutput, and CarExampleOutput) encapsulate the data returned by their respective endpoints, enhancing readability and maintainability.

public record ProductExampleOutput(String id, String name, double price,
                                   LocalDateTime dateTime) implements Serializable {
}

public record CustumerExampleOutput(String name, int age, LocalDateTime dateTime) implements Serializable {
}

public record CarExampleOutput(String name, String model, LocalDateTime dateTime) implements Serializable {
}

Conclusion

In summary, our journey through Spring Redis Cache has revealed powerful tools for boosting Spring Boot application performance. Leveraging caching annotations and configurations optimizes response times and reduces database load.

title: [Spring boot] How to use Web Socket with STOMP protocol.
content:
In this article we’re going to see how to implement web socket using Spring with STOMP protocol.

First of all, what’s Web Socket and when should I use it?

Well, Web Socket is a technology that makes it possible to open a bidirectional communication between the browser and server. The connection is established by sending an HTTP request from browser to a server to upgrade a connection and change the protocol. This operation is called Handshake.

The image bellow illustrates what was explained above.

When should I use Web Socket?

Use Web Sockets when you want two-way communication between two systems. Web Sockets are very useful for data visualization dashboards or maps that need to reflect real-time data values.

Creating Spring Application

We can use Spring Initializr to create a simple application with the Web Socket dependency like bellow.

After that, let’s create the necessary configurations to application runs correctly.

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WebSocketConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureMessageBroker(final MessageBrokerRegistry config) {
        config.enableSimpleBroker("/topic");
        config.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");
    }

    @Override
    public void registerStompEndpoints(final StompEndpointRegistry registry) {
        registry.addEndpoint("/websocket")
                .setAllowedOriginPatterns("*")
                .withSockJS();
    }
}

The annotation @EnableWebSocketMessageBroker tells to spring to enable the Web Socket message handling.

The class WebSocketConfig overrides some default configurations about Spring implementation that have two methods called configureMessageBroker and registerStompEndPoints.

The first one configures the message broker. Basically we enable a simple memory-based message broker. In this case, every client must subscribe to a topic prefixed with /topic to receive the messages and every message sent to server must be prefixed with /app.

The methodregisterStompEndPoints just register the Handshake end point and set all allowed origins.

Mapping received messages

In our example we will just receive a message by the client and return the same message to show in the browser. For that we will create a DTO to represent our message.


public class Message {

  private String content;

  public Message() {
  }

  public Message(String content) {
    this.content = content;
  }

  public String getContent() {
    return content;
  }

}

After the DTO is created, we need to create a Controller to receive and send to back the message.

@Controller
public class DemoController {


  @MessageMapping("/message")
  @SendTo("/topic/callback")
  public Message stompMessage(Message message) throws Exception {
    Thread.sleep(1000); // simulated delay
    return new Message("Returned by server, " + HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(message.getContent()) + " 💙");
  }
}

The code above uses our well-known @Controller annotation to Spring router our end-points.

The @MessageMapping it’s similar to the @RequestMapping when we are talking about HTTP requests. Then, every message that is sent to /message will be routed to stompMessage method.

On the other hand the @SendTo annotation will send the method return to a /topic/callback where the client is subscribed.

Creating the browser client

Let’s create a simple html file with some imports like: bootstrap, jquery, sockjs, and stompjs libs.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Hello WebSocket</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@3.3.7/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css" integrity="sha384-BVYiiSIFeK1dGmJRAkycuHAHRg32OmUcww7on3RYdg4Va+PmSTsz/K68vbdEjh4u" crossorigin="anonymous">
    <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.6.4.min.js" integrity="sha256-oP6HI9z1XaZNBrJURtCoUT5SUnxFr8s3BzRl+cbzUq8=" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/sockjs-client/1.6.1/sockjs.min.js" integrity="sha512-1QvjE7BtotQjkq8PxLeF6P46gEpBRXuskzIVgjFpekzFVF4yjRgrQvTG1MTOJ3yQgvTteKAcO7DSZI92+u/yZw==" crossorigin="anonymous" referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></script>
    <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/stomp.js/2.3.3/stomp.min.js" integrity="sha512-iKDtgDyTHjAitUDdLljGhenhPwrbBfqTKWO1mkhSFH3A7blITC9MhYon6SjnMhp4o0rADGw9yAC6EW4t5a4K3g==" crossorigin="anonymous" referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></script>
    <script src="/app.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
<div id="main-content" class="container">
    <div class="row">
        <div class="col-md-6">
            <form class="form-inline">
                <div class="form-group">
                    <label for="connect">WebSocket connection:</label>
                    <button id="connect" class="btn btn-default" type="submit">Connect 🙉</button>
                    <button id="disconnect" class="btn btn-default" type="submit" disabled="disabled">Disconnect 🙈
                    </button>
                </div>
            </form>
        </div>
        <div class="col-md-6">
            <form class="form-inline">
                <div class="form-group">
                    <label for="name">Type your message here 👋</label>
                    <input type="text" id="content" class="form-control" placeholder="Your message here...">
                </div>
                <button id="send" class="btn btn-default" type="submit">Send</button>
            </form>
        </div>
    </div>
    <div class="row">
        <div class="col-md-12">
            <table id="conversation" class="table table-striped">
                <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Greetings</th>
                </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody id="messages">
                </tbody>
            </table>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>
</body>
</html>

After that we need to create a Javascript file to makes possible the connection with our server. The code is very simple and I will comment just two functions.

var stompClient = null;

function setConnected(connected) {
    $("#connect").prop("disabled", connected);
    $("#disconnect").prop("disabled", !connected);
    if (connected) {
        $("#conversation").show();
    }
    else {
        $("#conversation").hide();
    }
    $("#messages").html("");
}

function connect() {
    var socket = new SockJS('http://localhost:8080/websocket');
    stompClient = Stomp.over(socket);
    stompClient.connect({}, function () {
        setConnected(true);
        stompClient.subscribe('/topic/callback', function (message) {
            showCallback(JSON.parse(message.body).content);
        });
    });
}

function disconnect() {
    if (stompClient !== null) {
        stompClient.disconnect();
    }
    setConnected(false);
}

function sendContent() {
    stompClient.send("/app/message", {}, JSON.stringify({'content': $("#content").val()}));
}

function showCallback(message) {
    $("#messages").append("<tr><td>" + message + "</td></tr>");
}

$(function () {
    $("form").on('submit', function (e) {
        e.preventDefault();
    });
    $( "#connect" ).click(function() { connect(); });
    $( "#disconnect" ).click(function() { disconnect(); });
    $( "#send" ).click(function() { sendContent(); });
});

The connect function creates a instance of SockJs passing the URL of the Handshake that is /websocket. Then we connect to the server and inside the success callback we subscribe in the topic /topic/callback.

The sendContent function sends the message to the server. It’s good to keep in mind the prefix /app that was configured previously.

Running the application

To run the back-end we can use some IDE like Eclipse or IntelliJ and to run the browser client we can use the VSCode with the LiveServer extension like the example.

Conclusion

In this post I have shared with you my experience using Web Sockets and Spring boot. I hope you have found the answers for your questions.

I will be happy to answer any questions you may have and the repo with all code you can find here: joseMarciano

title: [Spring boot] How implements integration tests using RabbitMQ and test-containers
content:
In this article, I will show you how you can implements integration tests using Springboot, test-containers and RabbitMQ.

First of all, we need create something to test. We can use the Spring Initializr

Create implementation for testing

After you create a project, we will create a service to send some message and a listener to consume that message.

Inside our build.gradle we will add the following dependency.

The dependency above has all we need to create a communication with RabbitMQ.

Service and Listener

With dependency above, we are be able to create our Service that will send a message and our listener that will wait for some message.

Let’s start with our listener.

@RabbitListener is an annotation that marks a method to be the target of a Rabbit message listener on the specified queues() (or bindings()).

Notice the id property in @RabbitListener . It’s important and I will tell why on the right moment.

Now, let’s create our publisher.

RabbitTemplate is a helper class that simplifies synchronous RabbitMQ access (sending and receiving messages).

Application.yml

The next step is to configure our application.yml to connect in RabbitMQ.

The application.yml was created with environment variables properties because we will override then in our tests. It’s a good practice create our application.yml with environment variables to set differents contexts like application-integration-test.yml, application-e2e-test.yml, etc.

Creating tests

For our tests, we will need some dependencies.

The following dependency is to create our RabbitMQ container. So, in every test, a docker container will up with a RabbitMQ instance.

Other important dependency is Awaitility. This library make easy asynchronous tests.

The last one and not less important, we need a dependency to make easy our test containers.

The next step is create our test class. Let’s create a simple Springboot test.

Now, we can annotate our test class with @Testcontainers and create our configuration for RabbitMQ container.

@DynamicPropertySource is to override the application.yml properties with the container configuration.

@Container is used for @Testcontainers to start the container. You can find more info about it here.

After create container configuration, we will inject the following Beans.

The first one is the RabbitAdmin . The purpose of this bean in our case, is to get some information about our queue.test .

The second one is the important because is where our listeners are registered. With this bean, we can listen or not some particular queue. In our case, we will stop to listen all queues and listen just the queue that we want to test.

The last one is our publisher that sends the message with Hello test .

Finally we can create the implementation of our test method.

Did you remember that the RabbitListenerEndpointRegistry is where the listeners are registered? So, in the line 1 we just stop all listeners to avoid side effects of others queues.

In the line 2 we create an assertion that ensures that we don’t have pending messages in the broker.

After that, in the line 3 we start listen the queue.test . Notice that the param passed togetListenerContainer is the ID’s listener.

In the line 4 we call our service that publishes a message to queue.test .

And finally in line 5 we create an assertion with awaitility that will check if the message has been successfully consumed. If 30 seconds have passed, the test should fail.

Conclusion

In this post I have shared with you my experience writing integration tests for RabbitMQ, Spring Boot and Test containers. I hope you have found the answers for your questions, the usage of the test containers and Awaitility library for testing asynchronous scenarios.

Surely there are many ways to solve this problem, so do not hesitate to share your experiences in the comments section.

Furthermore, I will be happy to answer any questions you may have!
